blocks.text: **The problem.** You're given a string as an **array of characters**, `s`. Reverse it **in place**: change the array itself, using only O(1) extra memory. Nothing is returned.

blocks.alt: The array h, e, l, l, o with a left pointer on h and a right pointer on o. Swap them: o, e, l, l, h. Move both pointers inwards and swap e with the second l: o, l, l, e, h. The pointers meet at the middle l, and the array is reversed.

blocks.text: Many string questions are about the string's two **ends** — reversing it, checking it reads the same both ways, comparing a character with its mirror. The two-pointer pattern puts one index at the **start** and one at the **end**, does something with the pair, and moves them **towards each other** until they meet. That visits each character at most once: O(n) time and O(1) extra space.

It's the first pattern because it's the simplest, and because it works on strings exactly as on arrays. The only string-specific part is the one from the immutability lesson: to change characters in place you need them in an **array** — which this problem hands you already.
Copy the characters, then write the copy back from the last character to the first. Simple, but the copy breaks the O(1)-memory rule.
**Time O(n), space O(n).** One pass to copy, one to write back — but the copy is as big as the input.
Swap the first and last characters, then the second and second-to-last, and so on. Each swap puts **two** characters in their final places, and nothing has to be stored except the two indexes.

blocks.caption: Each swap fixes two characters; the pointers meet in the middle.

blocks.text: **Time O(n), space O(1).** n / 2 swaps. With an odd length the middle character is never touched — it's already in place.

blocks.alt: Reversed copy: O(n) time, O(n) space. Two pointers: O(n) time, O(1) space.

blocks.text: Same speed, but only the two-pointer version meets the in-place requirement. Every language also has a built-in (`s.reverse()`, `s.reverse()`, `Collections.reverse`, `std::reverse`) that does exactly this swap loop.

items: **Empty array or one character** — the loop never runs; nothing changes.
**Even and odd lengths** — with an even length every character is swapped; with an odd one the middle stays.
**Using `left <= right`** — harmless here (it swaps the middle with itself), but `<` is the condition to remember.
**Reverse a String (immutable)** — when you get a real string, convert it to an array, run this, and join it back: still O(n).
**Reverse Vowels of a String** — the same two pointers, but each one first skips characters that aren't vowels.
**Reverse String II** — reverse the first k characters of every 2k-character block: the same swap loop on each block.
